title: Probability of union of two events
scenario_markdown: In a consumer market survey, 60% of respondents use Brand A ($P(A) = 0.60$), 50% use Brand B ($P(B) = 0.50$), and 30% use both brands ($P(A \cap B) = 0.30$). Find the probability that a randomly chosen consumer uses at least one of the two brands ($P(A \cup B)$).
assumptions: Fréchet inequality bounds satisfied: max(0, 0.6+0.5-1)=0.1 <= 0.3 <= min(0.6, 0.5)=0.5
Events are not disjoint because intersection is non-zero

approval.notes: Reviewed derivation: P(A union B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A cap B) = 0.6 + 0.5 - 0.3 = 0.80. Verified Frechet bounds and disjointness check.

stages.prompt_markdown: Which formula correctly gives the probability of the union $P(A \cup B)$?

options.hint_markdown: If you just add P(A) + P(B), what happens to the consumers who use both brands?
Multiplication relates to independent intersections, not unions.

stages.explanation_markdown: The general addition rule subtracts the intersection $P(A \cap B)$ because elements in both sets are counted twice when adding $P(A) + P(B)$.

stages.prompt_markdown: Calculate $P(A \cup B) = 0.60 + 0.50 - 0.30$. Enter as decimal, percent, or fraction.
Are events A and B mutually exclusive (disjoint)?

options.text_markdown: No, because $P(A \cap B) = 0.30 \ne 0$ (they have elements in common).
Yes, because their union is less than 1.0.
options.hint_markdown: What is the mathematical condition for disjoint events?

options.text_markdown: Yes, because disjoint is the same as independent.
options.hint_markdown: Disjoint means they cannot happen together; independent means one happening doesn't alter the chance of the other.

stages.explanation_markdown: Events are mutually exclusive (disjoint) if and only if $P(A \cap B) = 0$. Since $P(A \cap B) = 0.30 > 0$, they are not disjoint.
